title: en dynamei: "Son of God in power" or "declared ... with power"?
summary: The prepositional phrase en dynamei sits between huiou theou and the verb horisthentos, so it can qualify either the title ("Son-of-God-in-power") or the act of designation ("designated Son of God by/with power").

readings.label: Qualifies "Son of God": "Son of God in power"
readings.rendering: who was designated Son-of-God-in-power by the resurrection
readings.grammar: ἐν δυνάμει as an adjectival modifier of υἱοῦ θεοῦ (a new, enthroned status of the Son)
readings.modern: NIV, NET ("Son-of-God in power"); Cranfield, Moo

fathers.work: On the Predestination of the Saints
fathers.quote: Therefore Jesus was predestinated, so that He who was to be the Son of David according to the flesh should yet be in power the Son of God, according to the Spirit of sanctification, because He was born of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary.

readings.label: Qualifies the verb: "declared Son of God with power"
readings.rendering: who was powerfully declared to be the Son of God
readings.grammar: ἐν δυνάμει adverbial, with ὁρισθέντος (manner or means of the declaration)
readings.modern: KJV, NRSV ("declared to be Son of God with power")

fathers.quote: Thirdly, from the miracles which He did, yielding a demonstration of much power, for in power means this.

macula_evidence: MACULA gloss "declared son God with power" lists en dynamei after the participle phrase in a flat clause; the parse does not commit to either attachment.

title: kata pneuma hagiosynes: the Holy Spirit or Christ's own spirit?
summary: Paul sets "according to the flesh" (v. 3) against "according to the Spirit of holiness". The unusual phrase pneuma hagiosynes can refer to the Holy Spirit as agent of the resurrection or to the divine/spiritual sphere of Christ's own being.

readings.label: The Holy Spirit
readings.rendering: designated Son by the resurrection, according to (or through) the Holy Spirit
readings.grammar: πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης as a periphrasis for τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα (Semitic "spirit of holiness")

fathers.quote: Fourthly, from the Spirit which He gave to them that believe upon Him, and through which He made them all holy, wherefore he says, according to the Spirit of holiness. For it was of God only to grant such gifts.

readings.label: Christ's own divine nature
readings.rendering: designated Son of God as to his divine, spiritual nature (parallel to "flesh")
readings.grammar: κατὰ σάρκα / κατὰ πνεῦμα as a contrast of two spheres or natures of the one Christ
readings.modern: Commentators who stress the flesh/spirit contrast read it as two spheres of the one Christ

macula_evidence: MACULA parses κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης inside the ὁρισθέντος phrase, as a flat genitive phrase with no sign of which referent is meant.

title: hypakoen pisteos: "obedience to the faith" or "obedience that is faith"?
summary: The genitive pisteos after hypakoen (also 16:26) can be objective (obedience to the faith/gospel), epexegetic (the obedience which is faith), source (obedience that springs from faith), or subjective.

readings.label: Objective: "obedience to the faith"
readings.rendering: to bring about obedience to the faith (the gospel message)
readings.grammar: genitive of the object of obedience (ὑπακοή + objective genitive)
readings.modern: KJV ("obedience to the faith")

readings.label: Epexegetic/source: "the obedience of faith"
readings.rendering: to bring about the obedience which is faith (or comes from faith)
readings.grammar: epexegetic genitive or genitive of source; faith itself is the obedience
readings.modern: RSV, ESV, NAB ("the obedience of faith"); NIV 1984 ("obedience that comes from faith")

macula_evidence: MACULA gloss "to bring about obedience faith" notes the two nouns in sequence without labelling the genitive.

title: "from faith to faith"
summary: The two prepositional phrases ek pisteos eis pistin have no stated referent for either "faith", so the phrase has been read as a sequence of persons, of covenants, or of stages of growth.

readings.label: From the faith of the preacher to the faith of the hearer
readings.rendering: the righteousness of God is revealed from the faith of those who preach it to the faith of those who obey it
readings.grammar: ἐκ/εἰς marking source and goal of faith between two parties

fathers.work: On the Spirit and the Letter
fathers.quote: from the faith of them who preach it, to the faith of those who obey it.

readings.label: From Old Testament faith to New Testament faith
readings.rendering: revealed from the faith of the old covenant to the faith of the new
readings.grammar: ἐκ…εἰς as a progression from one dispensation to the next

fathers.quote: For after having said, from faith to faith, he sends the hearer back to the dispensations of God, which took place thus in the Old Testament, which, when writing to the Hebrews, he explains with his usual great wisdom, showing that both the just and the sinners were justified in that way even then,

readings.label: From God's faithfulness to human faith, or a growth in faith
readings.rendering: from God's faithfulness to human faith (or from one degree of faith to another)
readings.grammar: ἐκ πίστεως = God's fidelity; εἰς πίστιν = the believer's response (or intensive: "by faith alone")
readings.modern: Barth, Hays (faithfulness reading); NIV "by faith from first to last"

macula_evidence: MACULA treats ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν as two flat prepositional phrases modifying ἀποκαλύπτεται; no semantic link between them is encoded.

title: "The righteous by faith shall live" or "the righteous shall live by faith"?
summary: In the quotation of Habakkuk 2:4, ek pisteos stands between subject and verb and can modify either ho dikaios ("the one righteous by faith") or zesetai ("shall live by faith").

readings.label: Modifies the verb: "The righteous shall live by faith"
readings.rendering: the righteous person will live by means of faith
readings.grammar: ἐκ πίστεως adverbial with ζήσεται
readings.modern: KJV, NIV, RSV, ESV

fathers.quote: that it is not in the nature of things for him who is to live, to live otherwise save by faith; for the just, he says, shall live by faith, speaking about the life to come.

readings.label: Modifies the subject: "The one who is righteous by faith shall live"
readings.rendering: the person who is righteous through faith will live
readings.grammar: ἐκ πίστεως adjectival with ὁ δίκαιος (the theme of Rom 1-4 is justification by faith)
readings.modern: NET text, NRSV margin; Cranfield

macula_evidence: MACULA gloss "the righteous by faith live" attaches ἐκ πίστεως next to ὁ δίκαιος inside a flat clause; the parse does not commit.

title: dikaiosyne theou: the righteousness God has, gives, or requires?
summary: The genitive theou after dikaiosyne (1:17; 3:21-22; 10:3) can be possessive/subjective (God's own righteous character or saving covenant faithfulness), source (the righteousness God bestows on the believer), or objective (a status approved by God).

readings.label: Source: the righteousness which God gives
readings.rendering: a righteousness from God, given to the believer
readings.grammar: genitive of source/origin

traditions.catholic: Augustine's "righteousness by which He makes us righteous" underlies the Catholic doctrine of infused righteousness (Trent, session 6)
traditions.protestant: Luther: a righteousness from God received by faith

fathers.work: On the Spirit and the Letter
fathers.quote: This is the righteousness of God, which was veiled in the Old Testament, and is revealed in the New; and it is called the righteousness of God, because by His bestowal of it He makes us righteous, just as we read that salvation is the Lord's, because He makes us safe.

readings.label: Possessive/subjective: God's own righteousness
readings.rendering: God's own saving righteousness (covenant faithfulness) revealed in the gospel
readings.grammar: genitive of possession or subject; a divine attribute in action
readings.modern: Käsemann, N. T. Wright, Cranfield (partly)

macula_evidence: MACULA parses θεοῦ as an unlabelled genitive modifying δικαιοσύνη.

title: eis to einai autous anapologetous: purpose or result?
summary: εἰς τὸ + infinitive can express purpose ("in order that they be without excuse") or result ("so that they are without excuse"), which changes whether leaving humanity without excuse was God's intention in revealing himself.

readings.label: Result: "so that they are without excuse"
readings.rendering: so that they are left without excuse
readings.grammar: εἰς τὸ + infinitive of result (consecutive)
readings.modern: NET, NIV 1984 ("so that ... without excuse")

fathers.quote: And yet it is not for this God has made these things, even if this came of it. For it was not to bereave them of all excuse, that He set before them so great a system of teaching, but that they might come to know Him.

readings.label: Purpose: "in order that they be without excuse"
readings.rendering: in order that they should be without excuse
readings.grammar: εἰς τὸ + infinitive of purpose

macula_evidence: MACULA gives εἰς τὸ εἶναι as a flat infinitive phrase with no distinction of purpose/result.

title: physei: "do by nature" or "who by nature lack the law"?
summary: The adverbial dative physei can be taken with the verb poiosin (Gentiles do by nature the things of the law) or with the preceding participle phrase (Gentiles who do not by nature have the law). The choice decides whether Paul describes unaided nature or Gentile Christians.

readings.label: With the verb: "do by nature what the law requires"
readings.rendering: Gentiles who have not the law do by nature the things of the law
readings.grammar: φύσει modifies ποιῶσιν (instinctive obedience; or nature restored by grace)
readings.modern: RSV, NRSV, ESV, NIV ("do by nature"); Cranfield, Moo

fathers.quote: Do by nature the things of the Law. Of what Law? Of that by works.

fathers.work: On the Spirit and the Letter
fathers.quote: Nor ought it to disturb us that the apostle described them as doing that which is contained in the law by nature, — not by the Spirit of God, not by faith, not by grace. For it is the Spirit of grace that does it, in order to restore in us the image of God, in which we were naturally created.

readings.label: With the participle: "Gentiles who by nature do not have the law"
readings.rendering: when Gentiles, who by nature have no law (are Gentiles by birth), do what the law requires
readings.grammar: φύσει modifies ἔχοντα (lacking the law by birth/nature), so the doing is something beyond nature
readings.modern: A minority of interpreters

macula_evidence: MACULA places φύσει inside the clause with ποιῶσιν ("when gentiles ... by nature do the things of the law") and outside the relative clause τὰ μὴ νόμον ἔχοντα, so the tree encodes the "with the verb" reading.

title: "In the day when God judges" (2:16): which clause does it complete?
summary: The temporal clause of v. 16 follows a long parenthesis (vv. 14-15) and can be attached to the thoughts "accusing or excusing" of v. 15, or back to the judgment of v. 12-13 ("all who have sinned ... will be judged ... on the day").

readings.label: With v. 15: conscience and thoughts bear witness on judgment day
readings.rendering: their conscience bears witness, and their thoughts accuse or excuse them, on the day when God judges
readings.grammar: ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὅτε κρίνει completes ἐνδείκνυνται / the accusing-excusing clause of v. 15

fathers.work: On the Spirit and the Letter
fathers.quote: of what use will be their excusing thoughts to them in the day when God shall judge the secrets of men, unless it be perhaps to procure for them a milder punishment?

readings.label: With vv. 12-13: all are judged on that day (vv. 14-15 parenthetical)
readings.rendering: all who sinned will be judged ... on the day when God judges the secrets of men
readings.grammar: vv. 14-15 as parenthesis; v. 16 resumes v. 12 (κριθήσονται)

macula_evidence: MACULA gives v. 16 as its own sentence beginning ἐν ἡμέρᾳ with no syntactic link to v. 15 or v. 12.

title: proechometha: "Are we better off?" or "Are we at a disadvantage?"
summary: The form proechometha can be middle ("do we have an advantage?") or passive ("are we excelled / at a disadvantage?"), and with ou pantos ("not at all" or "not altogether"), giving different answers to the Jew's standing.

readings.label: Middle: "Do we (Jews) have an advantage?"
readings.rendering: What then? Are we better off? Not at all.
readings.grammar: προέχομαι middle, "to excel, surpass" (intransitive)
readings.modern: KJV, NIV, ESV, NRSV ("better off" / "better than they")

readings.label: Passive: "Are we excelled / at a disadvantage?"
readings.rendering: What then? Are we (Jews) at a disadvantage? Not altogether.
readings.grammar: προέχομαι passive, "to be surpassed"

macula_evidence: MACULA lists προεχόμεθα as a single finite verb without noting voice.

title: pistis Iesou Christou: faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ?
summary: The genitive Iesou Christou after pistis (also 3:26; Gal 2:16; Phil 3:9) can be objective (faith in Jesus Christ) or subjective (Jesus Christ's own faithfulness). The following phrase "to all who believe" supports the objective reading for some, redundancy for others.

readings.label: Objective: "faith in Jesus Christ"
readings.rendering: through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe
readings.grammar: objective genitive: Christ is the object of πίστις
readings.modern: RSV, ESV, NAB, NIV 1984 ("faith in Jesus Christ")

fathers.work: On the Spirit and the Letter
fathers.quote: But righteousness of God by faith of Jesus Christ, that is by the faith wherewith one believes in Christ for just as there is not meant the faith with which Christ Himself believes, so also there is not meant the righteousness whereby God is Himself righteous.

readings.label: Subjective: "the faithfulness of Jesus Christ"
readings.rendering: through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, for all who believe
readings.grammar: subjective genitive (or genitive of source): Christ's own faithful obedience
readings.modern: NET text ("through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ"), NRSV and ESV margin; Hays, Wright, Dunn (some)

macula_evidence: MACULA glosses διὰ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ as "through faith Jesus Christ" and does not label the genitive.

title: "through faith in his blood": what does en to autou haimati modify?
summary: The phrase dia pisteos en to autou haimati can be read as one unit ("through faith in his blood") or with en to haimati attached to hilasterion ("a propitiation by his blood, received through faith"). The Greek gives pisteos no object and the phrase may go with either.

readings.label: With hilasterion: "a propitiation in/by his blood, through faith"
readings.rendering: whom God set forth as a propitiation by his blood, through faith
readings.grammar: ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι adverbial/instrumental with ἱλαστήριον; διὰ πίστεως parenthetical
readings.modern: RSV, NRSV, NIV, ESV ("by his blood ... to be received by faith")

readings.label: With pisteos: "through faith in his blood"
readings.rendering: whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood
readings.grammar: ἐν τῷ αἵματι as the object of πίστεως ("faith in his blood")
readings.modern: KJV

macula_evidence: MACULA lists the whole chain διὰ πίστεως ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι as a flat string of prepositional phrases after ἱλαστήριον.

title: ton ek pisteos Iesou: "the one who has faith in Jesus" or "who shares Jesus' faith"?
summary: The expression ton ek pisteos Iesou, "the one of the faith of Jesus", has Iesou as the genitive of pistis. It can mean the one who believes in Jesus (objective), or the one whose standing rests on Jesus' own faithfulness (subjective).

readings.label: Objective: "the one who has faith in Jesus"
readings.rendering: that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus
readings.grammar: objective genitive after πίστεως
readings.modern: KJV, NIV, RSV, ESV ("faith in Jesus")

readings.label: Subjective: "the one who lives from the faithfulness of Jesus"
readings.rendering: ... the justifier of the one who lives from the faithfulness of Jesus
readings.grammar: subjective genitive
readings.modern: NET margin, NRSV margin; Hays, Campbell

macula_evidence: MACULA glosses the phrase as "the by faith Jesus" and does not mark the type of genitive.

title: Abraham "according to the flesh": what does kata sarka modify?
summary: In Rom 4:1 kata sarka can be linked to propatora ("our forefather according to the flesh") or to heurekenai ("found according to the flesh", i.e. by human effort). The infinitive heurekenai is itself omitted in some manuscripts.

readings.label: With propatora: "our forefather according to the flesh"
readings.rendering: what did Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, find?
readings.grammar: κατὰ σάρκα adjectival, modifying τὸν προπάτορα ἡμῶν
readings.modern: RSV, ESV, NAB, NIV 1984 ("our forefather according to the flesh")

readings.label: With heurekenai: "found according to the flesh"
readings.rendering: what did Abraham, our forefather, discover by his own human efforts?
readings.grammar: κατὰ σάρκα adverbial, modifying εὑρηκέναι
readings.modern: Hays

macula_evidence: MACULA lists κατὰ σάρκα as the last words of the clause with no marked attachment.

title: dia in 4:25: "because of" or "for the sake of"?
summary: Dia + accusative can be causal ("because of our trespasses ... because of our justification") or final ("for our trespasses ... for our justification"). The same preposition governs both halves, but each half may take a different sense.

readings.label: Retrospective in the first half, prospective in the second
readings.rendering: delivered up because of our trespasses, raised for the sake of our justification
readings.grammar: first διά causal (past sins), second διά final (to bring about justification)
readings.modern: RSV, NIV, ESV render "for" in both halves

fathers.quote: See how after mentioning the cause of His death, he makes the same cause likewise a demonstration of the resurrection.

readings.label: Retrospective in both halves
readings.rendering: delivered because of our trespasses and raised because we had been justified
readings.grammar: both διά causal; the resurrection follows an already accomplished justification

macula_evidence: MACULA lists both διά phrases as flat prepositional phrases with no marked sense.

title: he agape tou theou: God's love for us or our love for God?
summary: The genitive tou theou after agape can be subjective (God's love for us) or objective (our love for God), a difference that bears on the origin of love in the Christian.

readings.label: Subjective: God's love for us
readings.rendering: the love which God has for us is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit
readings.grammar: subjective genitive: God is the lover
readings.modern: NIV, NET, NRSV; Cranfield, Moo (the context speaks of God's love shown at the cross, 5:8)

fathers.quote: What things done? The Love which He has shown for us. In doing what? Some may say. In giving the Holy Ghost. Wherefore after saying hope makes not ashamed, he goes on to the proof of this, as follows: Because the love of God is, he does not say given, but shed abroad in our hearts, so showing the profusion of it. That gift then, which is the greatest possible, He has given; not heaven and earth and sea, but what is more precious than any of these, and has rendered us Angels from being men, yea sons of God, and brethren of Christ. But what is this gift? The Holy Spirit.

readings.label: Objective: our love for God
readings.rendering: love for God has been shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit
readings.grammar: objective genitive: God is the object of love

fathers.work: On the Spirit and the Letter
fathers.quote: Now the love of God is said to be shed abroad in our hearts, not because He loves us, but because He makes us lovers of Himself;

macula_evidence: MACULA leaves ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ as a noun phrase with an unlabelled genitive.

title: eph' hō: "because" or "in whom"?
summary: The compound eph' hō can be read as a conjunction ("because", "inasmuch as") or as a preposition plus relative pronoun whose antecedent is Adam ("in whom") or sin/death ("in which"). The Latin Vulgate in quo allowed both Adam and sin; the Greek Fathers read it causally.

readings.label: Causal: "because all sinned"
readings.rendering: death spread to all men, because all sinned
readings.grammar: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ as a conjunction (= ἐπὶ τούτῳ ὅτι)

traditions.orthodox: Greek patristic reading: death is inherited from Adam, guilt is each person's own

readings.modern: Most modern translations (RSV, NAB, ESV, NIV: "because")

fathers.quote: But what means, for that all have sinned? This; he having once fallen, even they that had not eaten of the tree did from him, all of them, become mortal.

readings.label: "In whom" (Adam): all sinned in him
readings.rendering: death spread to all, in whom (Adam) all sinned
readings.grammar: ᾧ as masculine relative with antecedent ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου (Adam)

traditions.catholic: Latin West, Augustine (in quo): basis of the doctrine of original sin, cited at Trent session 5

fathers.work: On Merit and the Forgiveness of Sins
fathers.quote: Why did death reign on account of the sin of one, unless it was that men were bound by the chain of death in that one man in whom all men sinned, even though they added no sins of their own?

readings.label: "In which" (the sin, or death)
readings.rendering: death spread to all, in which [sin] all sinned
readings.grammar: ᾧ as neuter relative: antecedent ἁμαρτία or θάνατος

fathers.work: On Merit and the Forgiveness of Sins
fathers.quote: Again, in the clause which follows, In which all have sinned, how cautiously, rightly, and unambiguously is the statement expressed! For if you understand that sin to be meant which by one man entered into the world, In which [sin] all have sinned, it is surely clear enough, that the sins which are peculiar to every man, which they themselves commit and which belong simply to them, mean one thing;

macula_evidence: The tree glosses ἐφ᾽ as "because" and heads the clause ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον as a relative under ἐφ᾽ with a bare "*" gloss on ᾧ; the gloss follows the causal reading.

title: "After the likeness of Adam's transgression": what does it modify?
summary: The phrase epi to homoiomati tes parabaseos Adam can modify "those who had not sinned" (they did not sin in the way Adam did) or the verb "reigned" (death reigned in the manner of Adam's sin).

readings.label: With "those who had not sinned"
readings.rendering: death reigned even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam's transgression
readings.grammar: ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι with τοὺς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας
readings.modern: ESV, RSV, NIV

fathers.work: On Merit and the Forgiveness of Sins
fathers.quote: even in those who had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, that is, who had not yet sinned of their own individual will, as Adam did,

readings.label: With "death reigned"
readings.rendering: death reigned from Adam to Moses, after the similitude of Adam's transgression, even over those who had not sinned
readings.grammar: ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι adverbial with ἐβασίλευσεν

fathers.quote: How did it reign? After the similitude of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of Him that was to come.

macula_evidence: The tree places ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδάμ inside the clause headed by μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας.

title: hina pleonase: purpose or result?
summary: ἵνα can express purpose ("the law came in in order that the trespass might increase") or result ("with the result that"). The choice decides whether increasing sin was God's aim in giving the law.

readings.label: Result: "so that the trespass increased"
readings.rendering: the law came in, with the result that the trespass increased
readings.grammar: ἵνα consecutive (ecbatic)

fathers.quote: But the particle that again does not assign the cause, but the result. For the purpose of its being given was not in order that it might abound, for it was given to diminish and destroy the offense. But it resulted the opposite way, not owing to the nature of the Law, but owing to the listlessness of those who received it.

readings.label: Purpose: "in order that the trespass might increase"
readings.rendering: the law came in in order that the trespass might abound (so that grace might abound more)
readings.grammar: ἵνα telic
readings.modern: KJV, RSV, NIV, ESV ("so that" / "in order that")

fathers.work: On the Spirit and the Letter
fathers.quote: For there was need to prove to man how corruptly weak he was, so that against his iniquity, the holy law brought him no help towards good, but rather increased than diminished his iniquity; seeing that the law entered, that the offense might abound; that being thus convicted and confounded, he might see not only that he needed a physician, but also God as his helper so to direct his steps that sin should not rule over him, and he might be healed by betaking himself to the help of the divine mercy;

macula_evidence: The tree marks ἵνα as the head of an adverbial clause with no purpose/result distinction.

title: "What fruit had you then?": where does the question end?
summary: The question can end after tote (what fruit did you then have? things of which you are now ashamed) or run on (what fruit did you have then from the things of which you are now ashamed?). The second makes the answer "none".

readings.label: One question: "fruit from the things of which you are now ashamed"
readings.rendering: What fruit were you getting then from the things of which you are now ashamed? (None; their end is death)
readings.grammar: ἐφ᾽ οἷς as part of the question, with εἴχετε
readings.modern: ESV, NIV, NRSV (one question)

fathers.quote: What fruit had ye then in those things whereof you are now ashamed? So great was the slavery, that even the recollection of it now makes you ashamed;

readings.label: Stop after tote: "What fruit did you have then? Things of which you are now ashamed"
readings.rendering: What fruit did you have then? The things of which you are now ashamed
readings.grammar: ἐφ᾽ οἷς begins the answer

macula_evidence: The tree keeps ἐφ᾽ οἷς νῦν ἐπαισχύνεσθε as a relative clause under εἴχετε in the same sentence as τίνα καρπὸν, i.e. one question.

title: Romans 7:14-25: who is the "I", and does the present tense matter?
summary: The present-tense first-person speaker is "carnal, sold under sin" yet delights in God's law. Readers divide over whether "I" is Paul before Christ, the regenerate Paul, or a representative figure (Adam, Israel, humanity under the law).

readings.label: Unregenerate: man under the law, before grace
readings.rendering: a portrait of the person (Paul or Israel) under the law without the Spirit
readings.grammar: ἐγὼ σάρκινός εἰμι as a vivid or dramatic present describing the pre-Christian state

traditions.orthodox: Greek Fathers generally (Chrysostom, Origen): the person under the law without grace

fathers.quote: giving us a sketch now of man, as comporting himself in the Law, and before the Law.

readings.label: Regenerate: Paul as a believer, struggling
readings.rendering: the Christian Paul, still carnal in his body, who nevertheless serves God
readings.grammar: present tense taken literally (εἰμί, not ἦν)

traditions.protestant: Luther and Calvin read it of the regenerate

fathers.work: Against Two Letters of the Pelagians
fathers.quote: He does not say, I was, but, I am. Was, then, the apostle, when he wrote this, carnal?

macula_evidence: The tree is flat for the clause (ἐγὼ σάρκινός εἰμι πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν) and does not encode who the speaker is.

title: "In Christ Jesus" (8:2): does it modify "the law of the Spirit of life" or "set you free"?
summary: The phrase en Christo Iesou can qualify the noun phrase "the law of the Spirit of life" (the law of the Spirit that operates in Christ Jesus) or the verb eleutherosen ("in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit set you free").

readings.label: With the noun phrase: "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus"
readings.rendering: the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free

title: kai peri hamartias: "as a sin offering" or "concerning sin"?
summary: The phrase peri hamartias, used in the Septuagint for the sin offering, can be a technical sacrificial term ("as a sin offering") or a general phrase ("because of / to deal with sin").

readings.label: General: "for sin" / "concerning sin"
readings.rendering: God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and to deal with sin

title: symmartyrei to pneumati hemon: "with our spirit" or "to our spirit"?
summary: The dative pneumati after symmartyrei can be a dative of association (the Spirit testifies together with our spirit) or a dative of the person addressed (the Spirit testifies to our spirit).

readings.rendering: the Spirit himself bears witness together with our spirit

readings.grammar: dative of the person addressed

macula_evidence: The tree glosses the verb with its dative as a flat clause and does not label the dative.

title: eph' helpidi: what does "in hope" modify, and is hoti "that" or "because"?
summary: The phrase eph' helpidi can be tied to "the one who subjected" (he subjected it in hope), or to the creation (it was subjected in hope). The following hoti can be "that" (the content of the hope) or "because" (the ground).

readings.label: With "the one who subjected it": "subjected it in hope"
readings.rendering: creation was subjected by the one who subjected it, in hope that it would be set free
readings.grammar: ἐφ᾽ ἑλπίδι with τὸν ὑποτάξαντα; ὅτι = "that"

title: panta synergei: what is the subject?
summary: Without an expressed subject, panta can be the nominative subject ("all things work together") or the accusative object of an understood subject God (or the Spirit): "he works all things together for good". (A textual variant adds ho theos; this entry is about the Greek of the shorter text.)

readings.label: Subject: "all things work together for good"
readings.rendering: all things work together for good for those who love God
readings.grammar: πάντα as nominative subject of συνεργεῖ
readings.modern: KJV, ESV

readings.rendering: God works all things together for good for those who love him
readings.grammar: πάντα accusative object; subject God (or the Spirit) supplied

title: "It is God who justifies": statement or question?
summary: Paul's series can be read as questions followed by answers ("Who will bring a charge? God, who justifies. Who condemns? Christ ...") or each second clause can be read as a rhetorical question ("Is it God who justifies? Who is it that condemns?"), which changes the sense.

readings.label: Question and answer
readings.rendering: Who will charge God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who will condemn? It is Christ who died.
readings.grammar: θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν as an affirmation answering τίς ἐγκαλέσει
readings.modern: RSV, NIV, ESV

fathers.quote: It is God that justifies. Ver. 34. Who is He that condemns?

readings.label: Chain of rhetorical questions
readings.rendering: Who will charge God's elect? Is it God, who justifies? Who is it that condemns? Is it Christ, who died?
readings.grammar: θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν as a second question expecting "no"

title: ēuchomēn: "I could wish" or "I was wishing"?
summary: The imperfect ēuchomēn can be a conative or unfulfilled-wish imperfect ("I could wish, if it were possible") or a true past ("I used to pray", in Paul's pre-conversion zeal).

readings.label: Conative/potential: "I could wish"
readings.rendering: I could wish (were it possible) that I myself were accursed from Christ
readings.grammar: imperfect of a wish that is not or cannot be realised
readings.modern: KJV, RSV, ESV ("I could wish")

readings.grammar: imperfect as a genuine past tense

title: Romans 9:5: is Christ called "God over all"?
summary: Unpunctuated, "ho on epi panton theos eulogetos eis tous aionas" can be a relative clause in apposition to Christ ("Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever"), a separate doxology to the Father after a full stop at sarka ("God who is over all be blessed forever"), or a doxology after a stop at pantōn ("who is over all. God be blessed").

readings.label: Apposition to Christ: "Christ, who is God over all"
readings.rendering: from whom is the Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever
readings.grammar: ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς εὐλογητός as a relative clause modifying ὁ χριστός
readings.modern: ESV, NIV, NAB, KJV text

fathers.quote: Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.
Moreover, he expressly called Christ God, saying: Of whom are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed forever.

readings.label: Full stop after sarka: doxology to the Father
readings.rendering: Christ came according to the flesh. God who is over all be blessed forever
readings.grammar: ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς εὐλογητός as an independent doxology (εὐλογητός precedes or follows)
readings.modern: RSV (1952) text; ESV, NRSV margin

readings.label: Full stop after pantōn
readings.rendering: ... who is over all. God be blessed forever
readings.grammar: θεὸς εὐλογητός a separate doxology

title: skeue orges katertismena: who fitted the vessels?
summary: The perfect participle katertismena can be passive (fitted by God), middle (having fitted themselves), or a passive without implied agent (ripe, ready for destruction). The voice decides whether God or the vessels prepared them.

readings.label: Middle: "having fitted themselves"
readings.rendering: vessels of wrath that had made themselves fit for destruction
readings.grammar: κατηρτισμένα as middle/reflexive in sense

fathers.quote: Wherefore he calls him not only a vessel of wrath, but also one fitted for destruction. That is, fully fitted indeed, but by his own proper self.

readings.label: Passive with God as agent: "fitted by God"
readings.rendering: vessels of wrath fitted by God for destruction
readings.grammar: κατηρτισμένα as a divine passive (contrast v. 23 "prepared beforehand" ἃ προητοίμασεν)

fathers.quote: For we find that some sins are even the punishment of other sins, as are those vessels of wrath which the apostle describes as fitted to destruction;

macula_evidence: The tree glosses the participle as a plain adjectival modifier of σκεύη ὀργῆς with no marking of voice or agent.

title: kai houtōs pas Israel sōthēsetai: "and so" or "and then"?
summary: The adverb houtōs normally means "in this way", but it has been read as "and then" (temporal sequence after the fullness of the Gentiles) or as "thus" (the manner: by Israel being provoked to jealousy).

readings.label: Temporal: "and then all Israel will be saved"
readings.rendering: after the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel will be saved
readings.grammar: οὕτως as sequence (a future mass conversion)

fathers.quote: When the fullness of the Gentiles, he says, shall have come in, then shall all Israel be saved, at the time of his second coming, and the end of the world.

readings.label: Manner: "in this way all Israel will be saved"
readings.rendering: in this way (by the process of vv. 11-25) all Israel will be saved
readings.grammar: οὕτως adverb of manner
readings.modern: Many modern commentators (Moo, Cranfield: "and so")

macula_evidence: The tree glosses οὕτως as "so" and sets it at the head of the clause with πᾶς Ἰσραήλ.

title: metron pisteos: what is "the measure of faith"?
summary: The genitive pisteos can be epexegetic (the measure is faith itself, given by God in different amounts), or a genitive of standard (a measure by which each is to judge) or a measure belonging to each one's faith.

readings.label: Epexegetic: God dealt faith as a measure to each
readings.rendering: God has apportioned to each a measure which is faith
readings.grammar: genitive of apposition: μέτρον = πίστις

fathers.quote: meaning here the gift by faith: and by using the word dealt, he solaces him who had the less, and humbles him who had the greater share.

readings.label: Standard: faith as the measure of self-judgment
readings.rendering: think soberly, as God has given each the standard of faith
readings.grammar: genitive of content/standard (πίστις as the criterion)

macula_evidence: The tree glosses μέτρον πίστεως as a flat noun phrase after ἐμέρισεν.

title: analogia tes pisteos: proportion of one's faith, or the rule of faith?
summary: The genitive pisteos can be subjective ("in proportion to one's own faith") or objective ("in accord with the faith", the body of belief), a distinction behind the later "analogy of faith".

readings.label: Subjective: in proportion to the prophet's faith
readings.rendering: let us prophesy in proportion to our faith
readings.grammar: genitive of the possessor; ἀναλογία = proportion

fathers.quote: For though it is a grace, yet it is not poured forth at random, but framing its measure according to the recipients, it lets as much flow as it may find the vessel of faith that is brought to be capable of.

readings.label: Objective: in agreement with the faith (the creed)
readings.rendering: let prophecy be in accord with the faith (the body of doctrine)
readings.grammar: objective genitive; ἀναλογία = analogy / conformity

title: tois tapeinois synapagomenoi: "lowly people" or "lowly things"?
summary: The dative tois tapeinois can be masculine ("associate with the lowly") or neuter ("be carried along with lowly things / humble tasks"); the verb synapagomenoi means "be led along with".

readings.label: Masculine: "associate with the lowly"

readings.grammar: τοῖς ταπεινοῖς masculine (persons)

readings.rendering: do not set your mind on high things but go along with humble things

title: dote topon te orge: whose wrath?
summary: The article-anarthrous dative te orge ("give place to wrath") does not say whose wrath: the angry person's own, the offender's, or God's.

readings.rendering: give place to the wrath of God

Now since what the injured man desires most to see is, himself having the pleasure of revenge, this very thing he gives him in full measure, that if you dost not avenge yourself, he means, God will be your avenger. Leave it then to Him to follow up your wrongs.

summary: The preposition en with the dative can be inclusive ("outstanding among the apostles", so Andronicus and Junia are apostles) or exclusive ("well known to / in the eyes of the apostles", so they are not). The question is bound up with whether Iounian is a woman (Junia) or a man (Junias).

readings.label: Inclusive: "outstanding among the apostles"
readings.rendering: they are prominent members of the circle of apostles

readings.modern: NIV, NRSV, RSV

fathers.quote: Then another praise besides. Who are of note among the Apostles. And indeed to be apostles at all is a great thing. But to be even among these of note, just consider what a great encomium this is! But they were of note owing to their works, to their achievements. Oh! How great is the devotion (φιλοσοφία) of this woman, that she should be even counted worthy of the appellation of apostle!

title: ten aparchen tou pneumatos: "firstfruits which is the Spirit" or "firstfruits from the Spirit"?

title: te elpidi esothemen: "in hope", "by hope" or "for hope"?
